To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the North-South model of the existing literature is not the only possible closure of the general framework, (2) alternative closures can generate a variety of outcomes for the terms of trade, and (3) these outcomes are sensitive to the closure chosen and to the assumptions made about the underlying model.

(1) the neoclassical model of North-South development is a "closure" that is not consistent with the other models examined in this paper and that is therefore not consistent with any other model in the existing NorthSouth literature, and (2) the neo-Keynesian and neo-Kaleckiana models of NorthSouth development are "closures" that are consistent with each other and are also consistent with the other NorthSouth models examined in this study.

(i) the North-South model with a fixed terms of trade is not a good representation of the world economy; (ii) the neoclassical North-South model, with a fixed terms or trade, is a good representation of North-South economic relations in the long run, and (iii) the North-Southern model, with a declining terms of trade, is not a good description of North-South relations in the long-run.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a broad class of underdetermined models in which alternative models can be viewed as providing alternative closures.

the following question: What are the implications for the North-South economic relationship of the different models of North-Southern trade and development that are currently being used in the literature?

the following issues: 1) the nature of North-South economic interdependence, 2) the nature of economic growth and development, 3) the nature of uneven development in North-South trade, and 4) the implications for long-run changes in North-South terms-of-trade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the existing models are not sufficiently general to provide a definitive answer to the question of whether North-South trade is likely to be a force for convergence or divergence.
the models examined here are not adequate for explaining long-run trends in the terms of trade, or for explaining long-run changes in patterns of North-South development.

the models examined in the paper provide a wide range of possibilities, and that it is impossible to predict with any certainty the future of North-South economic relations on the basis of the models examined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neo-Marxian and neo-Keynesian approaches are most likely to generate a pattern of uneven development in which the South is characterized by a low wage, low productivity, and low income economy.

the neo-Keynesian and neo-Kaleckians are more likely to lead to long-term improvements in the South's terms of trade, and that the neo-Marxian and neo-Kleins are more likely to result in long-term deteriorations in the terms of trade of both North and South.
, in general, the more "realistic" models of North-Sout h trade and development are, the more uneven the development and terms of trade patterns will be.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the North-South trade literature is characterized by a lack of consensus on the determinants of North-South income and trade patterns and on the long-run prospects for North-South trade.
the North-South models in the literature are not general enough to capture all of the relevant mechanisms that are important in explaining the North-South relationship.
alternative approaches to North-South trade can provide very different implications for development and for the terms of trade.
